A variety of [[processes]], [[equipment]], and [[materials]] are used in the production of a three-dimensional object via [[additive manufacturing]]. 

Techniques include jetting, [[Material extrusion-based additive manufacturing|extrusion]], additive friction stir deposition, [[powder bed fusion]], binder jetting, [[stereolithography]], [[computed axial lithography]], liquid alternative, lamination, [[Laser metal deposition|directed energy deposition]], selective powder deposition, and cryogenic manufacturing.

==Types==
3D printing processes, are grouped into seven categories by [[ASTM International]] in the ISO/ASTM52900-15:<ref>{{cite journal |date=2015 |title=Additive manufacturing — General Principles — Overview of process categories and feedstock |journal=ISO/ASTM International Standard |volume=17296-2:2015(E)}}</ref>

* [[Binder jetting]]
* [[Laser metal deposition|Directed energy deposition]]
* [[Material extrusion-based additive manufacturing|Material extrusion]]
* [[3D printing processes#Material jetting|Material jetting]]
* [[Selective laser melting|Powder bed fusion]]
* [[Sheet lamination]]
* [[3D printing processes#Stereolithography|Vat photopolymerization]]

Each process and piece of equipment has advantages and disadvantages associated with it. These usually involve aspects such as speed, costs, versatility with respect to [[Raw material|feedstock]], geometrical limitations and [[Engineering tolerance|tolerances]], as well as a mechanical and appearance properties of the products such as strength, texture, and color.

The variety of processes and equipment allows for numerous uses by amateurs and professionals alike. Some lend themselves better toward industry use (in this case the term [[additive manufacturing]] is preferred) whereas others make 3D printing accessible to the average consumer. Some printers are large enough to fabricate buildings whilst others tend to micro and nanoscale sized objects and in general many different technologies can be exploited to physically produce the designed objects.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bickel |first1=B. |last2=Cignoni |first2=P. |last3=Malomo |first3=L. |last4=Pietroni |first4=N. |date=2018 |title=State of the Art on Stylized Fabrication |url=http://vcg.isti.cnr.it/Publications/2018/BCMP18/StylizedFabricationSTAR_Personal.pdf |journal=Computer Graphics Forum |volume=37 |issue=6 |pages=325–342 |doi=10.1111/cgf.13327 |hdl=10453/129681 |s2cid=51870522 |hdl-access=free}}</ref>

==History==
[[File:Evolution_of_3D_Printing_Technologies.webp|thumb|604x604px|Evolution of 3D printing over the decades.<ref name=":43">{{cite journal |last=Sames |first=W. |year=2016 |title=The metallurgy and processing science of metal additive manufacturing |url=https://www.osti.gov/biblio/1267051 |journal=International Materials Reviews |volume=61 |issue=5 |pages=315–360 |bibcode=2016IMRv...61..315S |doi=10.1080/09506608.2015.1116649 |osti=1267051 |s2cid=39704506 |url-access=subscription}}</ref>]]
Inkjet printing was pioneered by Teletype which introduced the electrostatic pull Inktronic<ref name=":32">{{cite book |last=Webster |first=Edward |title=Print unchained: fifty years of digital printing, 1950-2000 and beyond: a saga of invention and enterprise |publisher=DRA of Vermont, Inc |year=2000 |isbn=0-9702617-0-5 |location=West Dover, VT |pages=116 |oclc=46611664}}</ref> teleprinter in 1966. The printer had 40 jets that offered a break-through speed of 120 characters per second.<ref name=":422">{{Cite book |last=Barnatt |first=Christopher |title=3D printing: the next industrial revolution |date=2013 |publisher=ExplainingTheFuture.com |isbn=978-1-4841-8176-8 |location=[Nottingham, England?] |oclc=854672031}}</ref>

[[Continuous inkjet|Continuous inkjets]] were popular in the 1950–1960's before [[Drop-On-Demand]]<ref>{{cite book |last=Kenyon |first=R.W. |title=Chemistry and Technology of Printing and Imaging Systems |date=1996 |publisher=Springer Netherlands |isbn=978-94-010-4265-9 |location=Dordrecht |pages=115–118 |chapter=Thermal printing |doi=10.1007/978-94-011-0601-6_6}}</ref> inkjets were invented in 1972.<ref>{{cite book |title=Chemistry and technology of printing and imaging systems |date=1996 |publisher=Blackie Academic & Professional |isbn=978-94-011-0601-6 |editor=Gregory, P. |location=London |oclc=669699931}}</ref> Continuous three-dimensional inks were wax based and low temperature [[Metal alloy|metal alloys]]. Printing with these [[Solid ink|hot-melt inks]] produced alpha-numeric characters that were solid and raised, but no one recognized them as 3D printing. In 1971, a young engineer, Johannes Gottwald patented a liquid metal recorder that printed large characters in metal for signage, but Teletype Corp ignored the discovery. Braille was printed with wax inks but never commercialized in the 1960s.

R.H. Research<ref>{{cite book |last=Howard |first=Robert |title=Connecting the dots: my life and inventions, from X-rays to death rays |date=2009 |publisher=Welcome Rain |isbn=978-1-56649-957-6 |location=New York |oclc=455879561}}</ref> researched printing from 1982 -1983 and decided that single-nozzle inkjet was a possible fit. He recruited engineers Al Hock, Tom Peer, Dave Lutz, Jim and Kathy McMahon to join the company, which became Howtek, Inc. The company's Pixelmaster device used [[ETFE|Tefzel]] nozzles, which allowed the inkjet to work at high temperature and support [[3D printing|thermoplastic]] hot-melt inks. The device could handle a frequency range of 1–16,000 drops per second. It featured 32 inkjet single nozzles per printhead, printing 4 colors (8 jets per color) [[CMYK]]. The printhead rotated at 121 rpm and placed uniform drops precisely as subtractive printing. This technology of hot-melt inks printing layers of CMYK was a precursor to a 3D patent by Richard Helinski.

Chuck Hull patented stereolithography (SLA) in 1986.<ref name="AutoSQ-162">{{US patent|4575330}}</ref>

In 1993, Helinski's patent was licensed first by Sanders Prototype, Inc.,(later [[Solidscape]], Inc) manufacturer of the first desktop rapid prototype printer, the Modelmaker 6 Pro. It used Howtek style inkjets and thermoplastic inks. Models printed with thermoplastic were perfect for investment casting with no ash during burnout. Thermoplastic ink drop printing is accurate and precise enough for jewelers and detail sensitive CAD designers. The Howtek inkjets that were designed to print a page in 4 minutes were employed to print for as long as 4 days straight.

==Processes==
Several 3D printing processes have been invented since the late 1970s.<ref name=":43" /> The printers were originally large, expensive, and highly limited in what they could produce.<ref name="3D opp2">{{cite news |author=Jane Bird |date=2012-08-08 |title=Exploring the 3D printing opportunity |url=https://www.ft.com/content/6dc11070-d763-11e1-a378-00144feabdc0 |access-date=2012-08-30 |work=[[The Financial Times]]}}</ref>

A large number of additive processes are now available. The main differences between processes are in the way layers are deposited to create parts and in the materials that are used. Some methods melt or soften the material to produce the layers, for example. [[selective laser melting]] (SLM) or [[direct metal laser sintering]] (DMLS), [[selective laser sintering]] (SLS), [[fused deposition modeling]] (FDM),<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ibrahim |first1=Yazan |last2=Hilal |first2=Nidal |year=2023 |title=The potentials of 3D-printed feed spacers in reducing the environmental footprint of membrane separation processes |url=https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jece.2022.109249 |journal=Journal of Environmental Chemical Engineering |volume=11 |doi=10.1016/j.jece.2022.109249 |s2cid=255328712 |url-access=subscription |article-number=109249}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hamzah |first1=Hairul Hisham |last2=Shafiee |first2=Saiful Arifin |last3=Abdalla |first3=Aya |last4=Patel |first4=Bhavik Anil |year=2018 |title=3D printable conductive materials for the fabrication of electrochemical sensors: A mini review |url=https://research.brighton.ac.uk/en/publications/bf3abba6-5c37-494f-8b6e-61f59938fdac |journal=Electrochemistry Communications |volume=96 |pages=27–31 |doi=10.1016/j.elecom.2018.09.006 |s2cid=105586826}}</ref>{{efn|FDM (Fused Deposition Modeling) is a trademark owned by [[Stratasys]]. Non-Stratasys machines using the same process are commonly referred to as using [[fused filament fabrication]] (FFF).}} or fused filament fabrication (FFF), while others cure liquid materials using different sophisticated technologies, such as [[stereolithography]] (SLA). With [[laminated object manufacturing]] (LOM), thin layers are cut to shape and joined (e.g., paper, polymer, metal). [[Particle deposition]] using [[inkjet technology]] prints layers of material in the form of individual drops. Each drop of solid ink from hot-melt material actually prints one particle or one object. Color hot-melt inks print individual drops of CMYK on top of each other to produce a single color object with 1–3 layers melted together. Complex 3D models are printed with many overlapping drops fused together into layers as defined by the sliced CAD file. Inkjet technology allows 3D models to be solid or open cell structures as defined by the 3D printer inkjet print configuration. Each method has its own advantages and drawbacks, which is why some companies offer a choice of powder and polymer for the material used to build the object.<ref name="Auto3D-72">{{cite news |last=Manolis Sherman |first=Lilli |date=November 15, 2007 |title=A whole new dimension – Rich homes can afford 3D printers |url=http://www.economist.com/theworldin/displaystory.cfm?story_id=10105016 |newspaper=The Economist}}</ref> Others sometimes use standard, off-the-shelf business paper as the build material to produce a durable prototype. The main considerations in choosing a machine are generally speed, costs of the 3D printer, of the printed prototype, choice and cost of the materials, and color capabilities.<ref name="Auto3D-82">{{cite web |last=Wohlers |first=Terry |title=Factors to Consider When Choosing a 3D Printer (WohlersAssociates.com, Nov/Dec 2005) |url=http://wohlersassociates.com/NovDec05TCT3dp.htm |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201104031948/http://wohlersassociates.com/NovDec05TCT3dp.htm |archive-date=2020-11-04 |access-date=2017-02-24}}</ref>

Printers that work directly with metals are generally expensive. However less expensive printers can be used to make a mold, which is then used to make metal parts.<ref name="Auto3D-92">{{cite web |date=2012-09-25 |title=Casting aluminum parts directly from 3D printed PLA parts |url=http://www.3ders.org/articles/20120925-casting-aluminum-parts-directly-from-3d-printed-pla-parts.html |access-date=2013-10-30 |website=3ders.org}}</ref>

=== Jetting ===

==== Material jetting ====
In material jetting a nozzle is drawn across an absorbent surface. The material is either [[Capillary action|wick]]<nowiki/>ed, electrostatically pulled from a larger jet,<ref name=":32" /> pressurized to expel material either continuously, or in short bursts as spray or drops.

Nozzles can be single nozzle with one fluid chamber or multi-nozzle with single or multi-fluid chambers, or combinations of these.

The material needs to have low enough viscosity to pass through the nozzle opening. Hot-melt materials can be melted to become liquid. The inks must be thick enough to accumulate vertically.

Continuous inkjet technology (CIT) began by printing signs and documents on paper, later adapted to print metals. Wax and thermoplastics were the first 3D materials, printed by drop-on-demand (DOD) inkjets.

==== Binder jetting ====
[[File:Schematic representation of granular binding fabrication.png|thumb|Schematic of binder jetting. Moving head selectively deposits binder onto powder bed. Platform lowers progressively. Solidified object rests in unbound powder. New powder adds from reservoir via leveling mechanism.]] 
Binder jetting deposits binding adhesive onto layers of powdered material.<ref>{{Cite web |title=3DEXPERIENCE Platform |url=https://make.3dexperience.3ds.com/processes/binder-jetting |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230403014128/https://make.3dexperience.3ds.com/processes/binder-jetting |archive-date=3 April 2023 |access-date=3 April 2023 |website=make.3dexperience.3ds.com}}</ref> Also known as inkjet 3D printing, the process spreads powder (ceramic, metal, or plastic-based, including plaster and resins) across a platform. A print head deposits binder in the cross-section of each layer. Modern printers cure (solidify) the binder at each layer. The resulting part is further cured in an oven to remove most binder. Operators sinter it in a kiln following a material-specific time-temperature curve. Unbound powder supports overhangs during printing. The method enables full-color prototypes and elastomer parts. Strength improves by impregnating voids with wax, thermoset polymer, bronze, or other compatible materials.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Doyle |first1=Michael |last2=Agarwal |first2=Kuldeep |last3=Sealy |first3=Winston |last4=Schull |first4=Kevin |date=2015 |title=Effect of Layer Thickness and Orientation on Mechanical Behavior of Binder Jet Stainless Steel 420 + Bronze Parts |journal=Elsevier Procedia Manufacturing |volume=1 |pages=251–262 |doi=10.1016/j.promfg.2015.09.016 |issn=2351-9789 |s2cid=138624845 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Make - Dassault Systèmes® |url=https://make.3dexperience.3ds.com/processes/binder-jetting |website=Make - Dassault Systèmes®}}</ref>
===Extrusion===
{{main|Fused deposition modeling}}
[[File:Schematic_representation_of_Fused_Filament_Fabrication_01.png|thumb|Schematic of fused filament fabrication. Filament '''a)''' feeds through heated moving head '''b)'''. Head melts and extrudes material, depositing it layer by layer to form shape '''c)'''. Moving platform '''e)''' lowers after each layer. Support structures '''d)''' sustain overhangs.]]
Fused filament fabrication (FFF), trademarked as fused deposition modeling (FDM), extrudes thermoplastic material to build objects layer by layer. As of 2023, FDM was the dominant 3D printing method.<ref name="auto3">{{cite web |last1=Palermo |first1=Elizabeth |date=19 September 2013 |title=Fused Deposition Modeling: Most Common 3D Printing Method |url=https://www.livescience.com/39810-fused-deposition-modeling.html |access-date=February 9, 2017 |publisher=Livescience}}</ref>

A filament of thermoplastic feeds into an extrusion nozzle. The nozzle head heats the material to its melting point and extrudes it onto a build platform. [[Stepper motor|Stepper]] or [[Servomotor|servomotors]] move the head and control flow along three axes. [[Computer-aided manufacturing]] software generates [[G-code]]. A microcontroller drives the motors.

Common materials include [[acrylonitrile butadiene styrene]] (ABS), [[polycarbonate]] (PC), [[polylactic acid]] (PLA), [[high-density polyethylene]] (HDPE), PC/ABS, [[polyphenylsulfone]] (PPSU), and [[high impact polystyrene]] (HIPS). The filament forms from virgin [[resins]].

===Additive friction-stir deposition===
Additive friction stir deposition (AFSD) is a solid-state metal additive manufacturing process that uses a rotating tool to deposit feedstock material onto a substrate.<ref>{{cite web |date=April 2018 |title=Non-beam-based metal additive manufacturing enabled by additive friction stir deposition |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/324276200 |access-date=August 20, 2024 |website=researchgate.net}}</ref> AFSD offers a number of advantages over other metal additive manufacturing processes, including high material utilization, low energy consumption, and the ability to print metal alloys incompatible with melt-based processes.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Anderson-Wedge |first1=K. |last2=Avery |first2=D.Z. |last3=Daniewicz |first3=S.R. |last4=Sowards |first4=J.W. |last5=Allison |first5=P.G. |last6=Jordon |first6=J.B. |last7=Amaro |first7=R.L. |date=2021 |title=Characterization of the fatigue behavior of additive friction stir-deposition AA2219 |journal=International Journal of Fatigue |volume=142 |bibcode=2021IJFa..14205951A |doi=10.1016/j.ijfatigue.2020.105951 |s2cid=225011973 |doi-access=free |article-number=105951}}</ref>

===Powder bed fusion===
{{main|Powder bed fusion}}
[[File:Schematic_representation_of_granular_binding_fabrication.png|thumb|Schematic of granular binding. Moving head '''a)''' selectively binds powder bed '''e)''' surface by dropping glue or laser sintering. Platform '''f)''' lowers progressively. Solidified object '''d)''' rests in unbound powder. Leveling mechanism '''b)''' adds new powder from reservoir '''c)'''.]]
[[Selective laser melting|Powder bed fusion]] (PBF) selectively fuses material in a granular bed.<ref name="auto12">{{cite journal |last1=Ibrahim |first1=Yazan |last2=Hilal |first2=Nidal |year=2023 |title=The potentials of 3D-printed feed spacers in reducing the environmental footprint of membrane separation processes |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S2213343722021224 |journal=Journal of Environmental Chemical Engineering |volume=11 |doi=10.1016/j.jece.2022.109249 |s2cid=255328712 |url-access=subscription |article-number=109249}}</ref> The process fuses layer parts, raises the working area, adds granules, and repeats until completion. Unfused powder supports overhangs and thin walls, reducing auxiliary supports. PBF includes [[Selective laser sintering|direct metal laser sintering]] (DMLS), [[selective laser sintering]] (SLS), [[selective laser melting]] (SLM), [[multi-jet fusion]] (MJF), and [[electron beam melting]] (EBM).<ref>{{Cite web |title=Powder bed fusion - DMLS, SLS, SLM, MJF, EBM |url=https://make.3dexperience.3ds.com/processes/powder-bed-fusion |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190410104731/https://make.3dexperience.3ds.com/processes/powder-bed-fusion |archive-date=10 April 2019 |access-date=10 April 2019 |website=make.3dexperience.3ds.com}}</ref> These methods handle diverse materials and enable complex geometries.

==== Selective laser sintering ====
[[Selective laser sintering]] (SLS) uses polymers and metals (e.g., PA, PA-GF, PEEK, [[alumide]], carbonmide, [[elastomers]]) and [[direct metal laser sintering]] (DMLS).<ref name="DMLS2">{{cite web |date=2014-03-03 |title=Aluminum-powder DMLS-printed part finishes race first |url=https://www.machinedesign.com/materials/metals/article/21831723/aluminum-powder-dmls-printed-part-finishes-race-first}}</ref><ref name="auto1">{{cite web |title=Selective Laser Sintering, Birth of an Industry - Department of Mechanical Engineering |url=http://www.me.utexas.edu/news/news/selective-laser-sintering-birth-of-an-industry |website=me.utexas.edu}}</ref> [[Carl R. Deckard|Deckard]] and Joseph Beaman developed and patented it in the mid-1980s under [[DARPA]] sponsorship.<ref name="auto1"/><ref name="Auto3D-32">Deckard, C., "Method and apparatus for producing parts by selective sintering", {{US patent|4863538}}, filed October 17, 1986, published September 5, 1989.</ref> R. F. Housholder patented a similar, uncommercialized process in 1979.<ref name="Auto3D-42">{{cite patent|country=United States|number=4247508|title=Molding Process|pubdate=27 January 1981|fdate=3 December 1979|inventor=R. Houshoulder}}</ref>

==== Selective laser melting ====

==== Electron beam melting ====
[[Electron-beam additive manufacturing|Electron beam melting]] (EBM) melts metal powder (e.g., titanium alloys) layer by layer with an [[electron beam]] in high [[vacuum]], producing void-free parts.<ref name="Auto3D-122">{{cite web |last=Hiemenz |first=Joe |date=9 March 2007 |title=Rapid prototypes move to metal components (EE Times, 3/9/2007) |url=https://www.eetimes.com/Rapid-prototypes-move-to-metal-components/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121102000116/http://eetimes.com/design/industrial-control/4013703/Rapid-prototypes-move-to-metal-components |archive-date=2012-11-02 |access-date=2024-10-17}}</ref><ref name="Auto3D-132">{{cite web |title=Rapid Manufacturing by Electron Beam Melting |url=https://www.smu.edu/Lyle/Centers/RCAM/Labs/RapidManufacturing/RMbyEBM |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150926003641/http://www.smu.edu/Lyle/Centers/RCAM/Labs/RapidManufacturing/RMbyEBM |archive-date=September 26, 2015 |publisher=SMU.edu}}</ref>

==== Multi-jet fusion ====
[[Multi-jet fusion]] (MJF) combines fusing and detailing agents with an inkjet array that it heats to solidify layers without lasers.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Material extrusion - FDM |url=https://make.3dexperience.3ds.com/processes/material-extrusion |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190209124107/https://make.3dexperience.3ds.com/processes/material-extrusion |archive-date=9 February 2019 |access-date=13 March 2019 |website=make.3dexperience.3ds.com}}</ref> Binder jetting spreads powder (plaster or resins) and prints binder via inkjet. Selective heat sintering applies heat with a thermal printhead to thermoplastic powder, offering a cheaper, scalable alternative.<ref name="auto">{{cite web |title=How Selective Heat Sintering Works |url=https://thre3d.com/how-it-works/powder-bed-fusion/selective-heat-sintering-shs |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140203071153/https://thre3d.com/how-it-works/powder-bed-fusion/selective-heat-sintering-shs |archive-date=3 February 2014 |access-date=3 February 2014 |publisher=THRE3D.com}}</ref>
Another 3D printing approach is the selective fusing of materials in a granular bed.<ref name="auto12" /> The technique fuses parts of the layer and then moves up, adding layers of granules and repeating the process until the piece is complete. This process uses the unfused media to support overhangs and thin walls, which reduces the need for auxiliary supports. For example, in [[selective heat sintering]], a thermal printhead applies heat to layers of powdered [[thermoplastic]]; when a layer is finished, the powder bed moves down, and an automated roller adds a new layer of material to [[Sintered|sinter]] into  the next cross-section; using a less intense thermal printhead instead of a laser, a cheaper solution than lasers, and can be scaled down to desktop sizes.<ref name="auto"/><ref name="Auto3D-122" /><ref name="Auto3D-132" />
===Vat photopolymerization===
[[File:Schematic representation of Stereolithography.png|thumb|Schematic of stereolithography. Light-emitting device '''a)''' (laser or DLP) selectively illuminates transparent bottom '''c)''' of tank '''b)''' filled with liquid photopolymer resin. Solidified resin '''d)''' drags up progressively by lifting platform '''e)'''.]] 
Vat [[Polymerization|photopolymerization]] cures liquid photopolymer resin layer by layer using light sources such as lasers, digital light projectors (DLP), or LEDs. The process exposes resin in a vat to controlled light under safelight conditions. Photopolymerization cross-links monomers, typically via carbon-carbon double bonds in acrylates, when exposed to chromophores or photosensitive additives.<ref name="pdcs2">{{cite journal |last1=Wang |first1=Xifan |last2=Schmidt |first2=Franziska |last3=Hanaor |first3=Dorian |last4=Kamm |first4=Paul H. |last5=Li |first5=Shuang |last6=Gurlo |first6=Aleksander |year=2019 |title=Additive manufacturing of ceramics from preceramic polymers: A versatile stereolithographic approach assisted by thiol-ene click chemistry |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/331309080 |journal=Additive Manufacturing |volume=27 |pages=80–90 |arxiv=1905.02060 |doi=10.1016/j.addma.2019.02.012 |hdl=1959.4/unsworks_60402 |s2cid=104470679}}</ref><ref name="Jacobs2">{{cite book |last=Jacobs |first=Paul Francis |url={{Google books|id=HvcN0w1VyxwC|plainurl=y}} |title=Rapid Prototyping & Manufacturing: Fundamentals of Stereolithography |date=1992-01-01 |publisher=Society of Manufacturing Engineers |isbn=978-0-87263-425-1}}</ref> The build platform moves incrementally. Excess liquid resin drains after completion. Objet PolyJet systems spray photopolymer in ultra-thin layers (16–30 μm). UV light cures each layer immediately, enabling instant handling without a later curing step. Gel-like supports are removed by hand or water jetting. 

The method suits elastomers and ophthalmic lenses.<ref name="Coward2015">{{cite book|author=Cameron Coward|title=3D Printing|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=N1cpBgAAQBAJ&pg=PT74|date=7 April 2015|publisher=DK Publishing|isbn=978-1-61564-745-3|page=74}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Butler Millsaps |first1=Bridget |date=6 March 2015 |title=Comparing LUXeXceL's Printoptical Technology to Transparent Polyjet, SLA & MJM 3D Printing |url=https://3dprint.com/49218/luxexcel-printoptical-clear/ |access-date=15 February 2018 |publisher=3DPRINT.com}}</ref>

[[Multiphoton lithography|Multiphoton polymerization]] uses focused lasers to cure gel only at focal points due to nonlinear photoexcitation. Excess gel washes away. This enables features under 100 nm and complex moving structures.<ref name="Auto3D-15">{{cite web |title=Cheaper avenue to 65 nm? (EE Times, 3/30/2007) |last=Johnson |first=R. Colin |date=30 March 2007 |url=https://www.eetimes.com/cheaper-avenue-to-65-nm/}}</ref> 

Mask-image-projection stereolithography slices models into planes, converts slices to masks, and projects them onto resin to cure layers. Some systems support multiple materials. 

[[Continuous liquid interface production]] (CLIP) uses an oxygen-permeable window below the resin pool to create a persistent liquid "dead zone." This enables continuous extraction of the object, reducing times from hours to minutes.<ref name="St. Fleur">{{cite news |url=https://www.theatlantic.com/technology/archive/2015/03/3d-printing-just-got-100-times-faster/388051/ |title=3-D Printing Just Got 100 Times Faster |last=St. Fleur |first=Nicholas |date=17 March 2015 |work=[[The Atlantic]] |access-date=19 March 2015 |archive-date=19 March 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150319200217/http://www.theatlantic.com/technology/archive/2015/03/3d-printing-just-got-100-times-faster/388051/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="St. Fleur2">{{cite news |last=St. Fleur |first=Nicholas |date=17 March 2015 |title=3-D Printing Just Got 100 Times Faster |url=https://www.theatlantic.com/technology/archive/2015/03/3d-printing-just-got-100-times-faster/388051/ |access-date=19 March 2015 |work=[[The Atlantic]]}}</ref><ref name="nat152">{{cite news |last1=Castelvecchi |first1=Davide |date=17 March 2015 |title=Chemical trick speeds up 3D printing |url=http://www.nature.com/news/chemical-trick-speeds-up-3d-printing-1.17122 |access-date=19 March 2015 |work=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]}}</ref> 

Dynamic Interface Printing (DIP) submerges a hollow print head with a transparent window into prepolymer. Visible light cures at the air-liquid [[Meniscus (liquid)|meniscus]]. Air pressure and acoustic modulation control the interface for precision and material flow. 

Preceramic polymers enable ceramic printing (e.g., [[silicon carbide]]) via photopolymerization.<ref name="pdcs2" /> Some systems solidify synthetic resin with LEDs.<ref name="Auto3D-16">{{cite web |title=The World's Smallest 3D Printer |date=12 September 2011 |publisher=[[Vienna University of Technology|TU Wien]] |url=http://amt.tuwien.ac.at/projekte/micro_printer |access-date=24 February 2017 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110920233607/http://amt.tuwien.ac.at/projekte/micro_printer/ |archive-date=20 September 2011}}</ref> 

Powder-fed directed-energy deposition melts supplied metal powder with a laser, a localized analog of selective laser sintering.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1007/s11837-015-1759-z |title=Review of Mechanical Properties of Ti-6Al-4V Made by Laser-Based Additive Manufacturing Using Powder Feedstock |journal=JOM |volume=68 |issue=3 |page=724 |year=2015 |last1=Beese |first1=Allison M. |last2=Carroll |first2=Beth E. |bibcode=2016JOM....68c.724B |s2cid=138250882}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |doi=10.1007/978-1-4939-2113-3 |title=Additive Manufacturing Technologies |year=2015 |last1=Gibson |first1=Ian |last2=Rosen |first2=David |last3=Stucker |first3=Brent |isbn=978-1-4939-2112-6 |url=https://ris.utwente.nl/ws/files/302088833/978_3_030_56127_7.pdf |archive-date=29 August 2023 |access-date=14 August 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230829172208/https://ris.utwente.nl/ws/files/302088833/978_3_030_56127_7.pdf}}</ref>

Vat [[Polymerization|photopolymerization]] is widely used for 3D printing of ceramic materials such as [[Aluminium oxide|alumina]] and [[Zirconium dioxide|zirconia]].<ref name="MinaryAlumina2024">{{cite journal |last1=Minary-Jolandan |first1=Majid |year=2024 |title=Vat Photopolymerization of Alumina: Effects of Slurry Properties and Printing Parameters |journal=Advanced Engineering Materials |doi=10.1002/adem.202400206}}</ref><ref name="MinaryZirconia2023">{{cite journal |last1=Minary-Jolandan |first1=Majid |year=2023 |title=3D-Printed Ceramics with Aligned Micro-Platelets |journal=ACS Applied Engineering Materials |doi=10.1021/acsaenm.3c00223}}</ref> Preceramic polymers also enable ceramic printing (e.g., [[silicon carbide]]) via photopolymerization.<ref name="pdcs2" />

The precision of ceramic vat photopolymerization is often challenged by light scattering and lateral overcure, which can obstruct fine internal features. Recent research has established quantitative frameworks for printing "vascular ceramics" with embedded internal channels. By optimizing cure depth-to-layer height ratios and applying geometric pre-compensation to account for symmetric tapering, fully enclosed channels can be achieved.<ref name="MinaryVascular2025">{{cite journal |last1=Alsup |first1=Zachary |last2=Minary-Jolandan |first2=Majid |year=2025 |title=Toward 3D printed “vascular ceramics” with vat photopolymerization: Determining the minimum printable open channel size |journal=Ceramics International |doi=10.1016/j.ceramint.2025.12.495}}</ref>

=== Computed axial lithography ===
[[Computed axial lithography]] reverses the principle of [[CT scan|computed tomography (CT)]] to create prints in photo-curable resin. It was developed by a collaboration between the [[University of California, Berkeley]] with [[Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory]].<ref name=":02">{{cite journal |last1=Kelly |first1=Brett E. |last2=Bhattacharya |first2=Indrasen |last3=Heidari |first3=Hossein |last4=Shusteff |first4=Maxim |last5=Spadaccini |first5=Christopher M. |last6=Taylor |first6=Hayden K. |date=2019-01-31 |title=Volumetric additive manufacturing via tomographic reconstruction |journal=Science |language=en |volume=363 |issue=6431 |pages=1075–1079 |bibcode=2019Sci...363.1075K |doi=10.1126/science.aau7114 |issn=0036-8075 |pmid=30705152 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name=":12">{{cite web |date=2019-01-31 |title=Star Trek–like replicator creates entire objects in minutes |url=https://www.science.org/content/article/star-trek-replicator-creates-entire-objects-minutes |access-date=2019-01-31 |website=Science |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":22">{{cite arXiv |eprint=1705.05893 |class=cs.GR |first1=Brett |last1=Kelly |first2=Indrasen |last2=Bhattacharya |title=Computed Axial Lithography (CAL): Toward Single Step 3D Printing of Arbitrary Geometries |date=2017-05-16 |last3=Shusteff |first3=Maxim |last4=Panas |first4=Robert M. |last5=Taylor |first5=Hayden K. |last6=Spadaccini |first6=Christopher M.}}</ref> It creates objects using a series of 2D images projected onto a cylinder of resin.<ref name=":02" /><ref name=":12" /><ref name=":22" /> It is notable for its ability to build objects more quickly than other resin methods and can embed objects within the prints.<ref name=":02" />

===Directed energy deposition (DED)===
====Powder-fed directed-energy deposition====
A high-power laser melts metal powder supplied to the focus of the laser beam. The laser beam typically travels through the center of the deposition head and is lens-focused to a small spot. The build occurs on an [[X-Y table]] which is driven by a tool path created from a digital model. The deposition head is moved vertically as each layer is completed. 

Some systems make use of 5-axis<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Yang |first1=Y. |last2=Gong |first2=Y. |last3=Qu |first3=S. |date=2019 |title=Additive/subtractive hybrid manufacturing of 316L stainless steel powder: Densification, microhardness and residual stress |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12206-019-1126-z |journal=J Mech Sci Technol |volume=33 |issue=12 |pages=5797–5807 |doi=10.1007/s12206-019-1126-z |s2cid=214298577 |url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Boisselier |first1=D. |last2=Sankaré |first2=S. |last3=Engel |first3=T. |date=2014 |title=Improvement of the Laser Direct Metal Deposition Process in 5-axis Configuration |journal=Physics Procedia |volume=56 |issue=8th International Conference on Laser Assisted Net Shape Engineering LANE 2014 |pages=239–249 |bibcode=2014PhPro..56..239B |doi=10.1016/j.phpro.2014.08.168 |s2cid=109491084 |doi-access=free}}</ref> or 6-axis systems<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Li |first1=L. |last2=Haghighi |first2=A. |last3=Yang |first3=Y. |date=2018 |title=A novel 6-axis hybrid additive-subtractive manufacturing process: Design and case studies |journal=Journal of Manufacturing Processes |volume=33 |pages=150–160 |doi=10.1016/j.jmapro.2018.05.008 |s2cid=139579311 |doi-access=free}}</ref> (''i.e.'' [[Articulated robot|articulated arms]]) capable of delivering material on the substrate (a printing bed, or a pre-existing part)<ref>{{cite web |date=17 July 2020 |title=Adding Features with DED |url=https://addupsolutions.com/applications/isogrid-case-study/ |access-date=17 January 2025 |website=AddUp}}</ref> with few to no spatial access restrictions. Metal powder is delivered and distributed around the head or can be split by an internal manifold and delivered through nozzles arranged around the deposition head. A hermetically sealed chamber filled with inert gas or a local inert shroud gas (sometimes combined) are often used to shield the melt pool from atmospheric oxygen, to limit [[Redox|oxidation]] and better control material properties. 

The powder-fed directed-energy process is similar to [[selective laser sintering]], but the metal powder is projected only where material is to be added to the part at that moment. The laser heats and creates a "melt pool" on the substrate, in which the new powder is injected quasi-simultaneously. 

The process supports materials including titanium, stainless steel, aluminum, tungsten, and other specialty materials as well as composites and functionally graded material. The process can build new metal parts, but can also add material to existing parts, supporting coatings, repair, and hybrid manufacturing applications. [[Laser engineered net shaping|LENS]] (Laser Engineered Net Shaping), is one example.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Beese |first1=Allison M. |last2=Carroll |first2=Beth E. |date=2015-12-21 |title=Review of Mechanical Properties of Ti-6Al-4V Made by Laser-Based Additive Manufacturing Using Powder Feedstock |journal=JOM |volume=68 |issue=3 |pages=724–734 |bibcode=2016JOM....68c.724B |doi=10.1007/s11837-015-1759-z |issn=1047-4838 |s2cid=138250882}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Gibson |first1=Ian |url=https://ris.utwente.nl/ws/files/302088833/978_3_030_56127_7.pdf |title=Additive Manufacturing Technologies - Springer |last2=Rosen |first2=David |last3=Stucker |first3=Brent |year=2015 |isbn=978-1-4939-2112-6 |chapter=Chapter 10 |doi=10.1007/978-1-4939-2113-3 |s2cid=114833020}}</ref>

===Selective powder deposition===
In selective powder deposition (SPD), build and support powders are selectively deposited into a crucible, such that the build powder takes the shape of the desired object and support powder fills the rest of the crucible. Then an infill material is applied, such that it comes in contact with the build powder. Then the crucible is fired in a kiln between the melting point of the infill and the powders. When the infill melts, it soaks the build powder. But it doesn't soak the support powder, because the support powder is chosen to not be wettable by the infill. If at the firing temperature, the atoms of the infill material and the build powder are mutually defusable, such as with copper powder and zinc infill, then the resulting material is a uniform mixture of those atoms, in this case, bronze. But if the atoms are not mutually defusable, such as tungsten and copper at 1100°C, then the resulting material is a composite. To prevent shape distortion, the firing temperature must be below the [[Liquidus and solidus|solidus temperature]] of the resulting alloy.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Magalhães |first1=Samuel |last2=Sardinha |first2=Manuel |last3=Vicente |first3=Carlos |last4=Leite |first4=Marco |last5=Ribeiro |first5=Relógio |last6=Vaz |first6=Maria |last7=Reis |first7=Luís |date=2021-08-23 |title=Validation of a low-cost selective powder deposition process through the characterization of tin bronze specimens |journal=The Journal of Materials: Design and Applications |volume=235 |issue=12 |pages=2681–2691 |doi=10.1177/14644207211031941 |s2cid=238738655}}</ref>

=== Electrochemical ===
Electrochemical additive manufacturing (ECAM) is as a cluster of technologies with the potential to fabricate 3D micro/nanostructures within diverse  materials. ECAM technologies include localized electrochemical deposition (LED), meniscus-confined electrodeposition (MCED), electrohydrodynamic redox printing (EHD-RP), fluid FM electrodeposition, and scanning ion conductance microscopy (SICM).  The [[electrolyte]] of a target metal is placed inside a glass capillary pipette. An electronic-ionic circuit is formed by a liquid capillary created between the pipette's tip and the conductive substrate. Metal ions [[Redox|reduce]] (release oxygen) when a voltage is applied and deposit on the substrate. Precision positioners control the pipette in three dimensions, creating the necessary three-dimensional objects. Manufacturing happens at nearl room temperature and produces fewer thermal defects.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Siddiqui |first1=Hafsa |last2=Singh |first2=Netrapal |last3=Naidu |first3=Palash |last4=Bhavani Srinivas Rao |first4=Kolayada |last5=Gupta |first5=Shaily |last6=Srivastava |first6=Avanish Kumar |last7=Santosh |first7=M.S |last8=Natarajan |first8=Sathish |last9=Kumar |first9=Surender |last10=Dumée |first10=Ludovic F. |last11=Rtim |first11=Sami |date=2023-11-01 |title=Emerging electrochemical additive manufacturing technology for advanced materials: Structures and applications |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1369702123003371 |journal=Materials Today |language=en-US |volume=70 |pages=161–192 |doi=10.1016/j.mattod.2023.10.008 |issn=1369-7021}}</ref> It permits feature resolutions in the 30-50 micrometer range. ECAM is under consideration as a technique for manufacturing advanced copper cooling plates for data centers that provide 98% reductions in energy consumption for cooling.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Uko |first=Etiido |date=2026-05-20 |title=Cooling copper plates could slash data center energy use by 90% |url=https://newatlas.com/energy/cooling-copper-plates-data-center-energy-use/ |access-date=2026-05-24 |website=New Atlas |language=en-US}}</ref>

==Printers==
===Industry ===
As of October 2012, additive manufacturing systems ranged from $2,000 to $500,000 in price and were employed in industries including aerospace, architecture, automotive, defense, and medical replacements. These devices are used for prototyping, jig making, fixturing, fixing small custom components, and complete products.<ref name="Wohlers, Terry 20162">{{Cite web |last=Wohlers |first=Terry |date=2016 |title=Wohlers Report 2016 |url=https://wohlersassociates.com/product/wohlers-report-2016/ |access-date=2026-01-11 |website=Wohlers Associates |language=en-US}}</ref>

Higher end 3-D printers have now become relatively common for production and [[additive manufacturing]].<ref name="Wohlers, Terry 20162" /> For example, [[General Electric]] uses additive manufacturing to build [[turbine]] parts. Rapid prototyping saves time and reduces complexity. Volkswagen uses 3D printers to print tooling, jigs and fixtures. As of 2018 they estimated that 3D printers save €250,000 per year in costs.<ref>{{cite news |last=O'Connor |first=Daniel |date=2018-02-22 |title=Can you jig it? 3D printing inside Volkswagen Autoeuropa |url=https://www.tctmagazine.com/can-you-jig-it-volkswagen-ultimaker-3d-printing/ |access-date=2018-11-28 |work=TCT Magazine |language=en-gb}}</ref> One 2018 report estimated that almost 75% of desktop 3D printers made are used in industry.<ref>{{cite news |last=Griffiths |first=Laura |date=2018-11-22 |title=How desktop 3D printers became an essential industry tool |url=https://www.tctmagazine.com/3d-printing-news/desktop-3d-printing-essential-industrial-tool/ |access-date=2018-11-28 |work=TCT Magazine |language=en-gb}}</ref>

Military and defense systems also incorporating the use of 3D printers. The [[Royal Netherlands Air Force]] is using desktop 3D printers to make fixtures and alignment tools.<ref>{{cite web |date=2019-01-11 |title=Royal Netherlands Air Force recruits Ultimaker 3D printers for maintenance and repair operations |url=https://3dprintingindustry.com/news/royal-netherlands-air-force-recruits-ultimaker-3d-printers-for-maintenance-and-repair-operations-146922/ |access-date=2019-01-11 |website=3D Printing Industry |language=en-US}}</ref> [[Hill Air Force Base]] uses 3D printed parts to replace jet parts.<ref>{{cite web |date=2018-07-27 |title=F-35 stealth fighter gets boost from 3D printing |url=https://3dprintingindustry.com/news/f-35-stealth-fighter-gets-boost-from-3d-printing-137138/ |access-date=2019-01-11 |website=3D Printing Industry |language=en-US}}</ref>

Higher education is a major buyer of desktop and professional 3D printers.<ref>{{cite web |date=2 December 2015 |title=Despite Market Woes, 3D Printing Has a Future Thanks to Higher Education - Bold |url=http://bold.global/jordan-brehove/2015/12/02/despite-market-woes-3d-printing-has-a-future-thanks-to-higher-education/}}</ref> In higher education, 3D printing is used to fabricate equipment. For example, chemists can 3D print flow reactor systems that would otherwise exceed typical budgets,<ref>{{cite web |last=Butler O'Neal |first=Bridget |date=2019-03-12 |title=UCL School of Pharmacy: 3D Prints Affordable Continuous Flow Systems |url=https://3dprint.com/238149/ucl-school-of-pharmacy-3d-prints-affordable-continuous-flow-systems/ |access-date=2019-03-12 |website=3DPrint.com {{!}} The Voice of 3D Printing / Additive Manufacturing |language=en-US}}</ref> such as a device created at the UCL School of Pharmacy in the UK.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hilton |first1=Stephen |last2=Peniche |first2=Bruno |last3=Rao |first3=Zenobia |last4=Penny |date=2019-02-28 |title=Modular 3D Printed Compressed Air Driven Continuous-Flow Systems for Chemical Synthesis |url=https://chemrxiv.org/articles/Modular_3D_Printed_Compressed_Air_Driven_Continuous-Flow_Systems_for_Chemical_Synthesis/7781033 |journal=[[ChemRxiv]] |language=en |doi=10.26434/chemrxiv.7781033.v1 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Many libraries house smaller 3D printers for educational and community access.<ref>{{cite web |title=UMass Amherst Library Opens 3-D Printing Innovation Center |url=http://lj.libraryjournal.com/2015/03/technology/umass-amherst-library-opens-3d-printing-innovation-center/#_ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402221847/http://lj.libraryjournal.com/2015/03/technology/umass-amherst-library-opens-3d-printing-innovation-center/#_ |archive-date=2015-04-02 |access-date=2017-02-24}}</ref>

===Consumer ===
[[File:RepRap_'Mendel'.jpg|thumb|[[RepRap Project|RepRap]] version 2.0 (Mendel)]]
[[File:First_replication.jpg|thumb|All of the plastic parts for the machine on the right were produced by the machine on the left. [[Adrian Bowyer]] (left) and Vik Olliver (right) are members of the [[RepRap project]].]]
[[Do it yourself|DIY]]/[[Maker culture|Maker]]/enthusiast/[[early adopter]] communities, with ties to the academic and [[Hacker (hobbyist)|hacker]] communities, led consumer-level adoption.

[[RepRap Project]] is one of the longest running desktop projects. It aims to produce a [[free and open source hardware]] (FOSH) 3D printer, under the [[GNU General Public License]] that is capable of replicating itself by printing many of its own parts. RepRaps can print [[Circuit board|circuit boards]] and metal parts. As of 2016, the most popular 3D printer was the [[Prusa i3]], a RepRap printer.<ref>{{cite web |title=3D Printing Trends July 2016 |url=https://www.3dhubs.com/trends |access-date=2016-07-12 |website=3D Hubs}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |date=2016-03-02 |title=What's up with Original Prusa i3? - Prusa Printers |url=https://blog.prusa3d.com/whats-up-with-original-prusa-i3_4124/ |access-date=2016-07-12}}</ref>

Many related projects have used RepRap for inspiration, creating an ecosystem of related or derivative 3D printers, most of which are also open-source. Development of open source 3D printers enables greater customization and the use of [[public domain]] designs to fabricate [[open source appropriate technology]]. 

The cost of 3D printers decreased dramatically after about 2010, with machines that used to cost $20,000 falling below $1,000. The open source [[Fab@Home]] project has developed printers for general use with anything that can be squirted through a nozzle, from chocolate to silicone sealant and chemical reactants. 

In addition, several [[RecycleBot|RecycleBots]] such as the commercialized Filastruder have been designed and fabricated to convert waste plastic, such as shampoo containers and milk jugs, into inexpensive RepRap filament.

===Microscale and nanoscale printers===
Microelectronic device fabrication methods can be employed to print nanoscale objects. Such printed objects are typically grown on a substrate, e.g., a silicon wafer, to which they adhere after printing as they are too small and fragile to be manipulated post-deposition.

In one technique, 3D nanostructures are printed by moving a dynamic stencil mask during the deposition process, somewhat analogous to the extrusion method of traditional 3D printers. Programmable-height nanostructures with resolutions as small as 10 nm have been produced in this fashion, by metallic physical [[vapor deposition]] using a mechanical piezo-actuator controlled stencil mask having a milled nanopore in a [[silicon nitride]] membrane.<ref name="wasserman082">{{cite journal |author=J. L. Wasserman |display-authors=etal |date=2008 |title=Fabrication of One-Dimensional Programmable-Height Nanostructures via Dynamic Stencil Deposition |journal=[[Review of Scientific Instruments]] |volume=79 |issue=7 |pages=073909–073909–4 |arxiv=0802.1848 |bibcode=2008RScI...79g3909W |doi=10.1063/1.2960573 |pmid=18681718 |s2cid=9775171 |article-number=073909}}</ref>

Another method enhances the photopolymerization process on a much smaller scale, using finely-focused lasers controlled by adjustable mirrors. This method produced objects with feature resolutions of 100 nm as of 2013.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Patel |first1=Prachi |date=5 March 2013 |title=Micro 3-D Printer Creates Tiny Structures in Seconds |url=https://www.technologyreview.com/2013/03/05/253621/micro-3-d-printer-creates-tiny-structures-in-seconds/ |work=MIT Technology Review}}</ref> Onr micron -wide, millimetre-long copper wires have been printed using lasers.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Grant-Jacob |first1=James A. |last2=Mills |first2=Benjamin |last3=Feinaeugle |first3=Matthias |last4=Sones |first4=Collin L. |last5=Oosterhuis |first5=Gerrit |last6=Hoppenbrouwers |first6=Marc B. |last7=Eason |first7=Robert W. |date=2013-06-01 |title=Micron-scale copper wires printed using femtosecond laser-induced forward transfer with automated donor replenishment |url=https://eprints.soton.ac.uk/356441/1/ome-3-6-747.pdf |journal=Optical Materials Express |language=EN |volume=3 |issue=6 |pages=747 |bibcode=2013OMExp...3..747G |doi=10.1364/ome.3.000747 |issn=2159-3930 |doi-access=free}}</ref>
